items.title: Anselm's ontological argument is a priori

options.text: An empirical argument from observation of nature
God is 'that than which no greater can be conceived'; existence in reality is greater than existence in the mind alone; therefore the greatest conceivable being must exist in reality
A historical argument from biblical events

items.reveal:
Anselm wrote the Proslogion (1077-78) as a contemplation aimed at finding 'a single argument' to prove God's existence. The famous formula appears in Proslogion 2.

Gaunilo (Anselm's contemporary) objected with his 'lost island' parody: by the same logic, the greatest conceivable island must exist. Anselm replied that the argument applies only to a necessary being, not contingent ones.

Descartes (Meditations V), Spinoza, Leibniz and Hegel reformulated versions. Kant's critique — existence is not a predicate (Critique of Pure Reason, 1781) — is the standard counter. Alvin Plantinga's modal version (1974) revived the argument using possible-world semantics.
items.why: The ontological argument is uniquely controversial. Almost everyone has the intuition that something is wrong with it — but the precise diagnosis (Gaunilo's? Kant's? Modal logic?) is itself contested philosophy.

items.title: Hindu philosophy teaches the unity of atman and Brahman
items.claim: What is the relationship between atman and Brahman in Vedantic Hinduism?

options.text: They are completely separate — the soul and a creator god

The Upanishads teach that atman (the individual self) and Brahman (ultimate reality) are one — 'tat tvam asi' ('that thou art', Chandogya Upanishad). Different Vedanta schools interpret the relationship variously (non-dual, qualified non-dual, dualist)
Atman is illusion; only Brahman is real, with no relation between them
Brahman is a god subordinate to atman

items.reveal:
The Mahavakyas ('great sayings') include 'tat tvam asi' (Chandogya 6.8.7), 'aham brahmasmi' (Brihadaranyaka 1.4.10) and 'ayam atma brahma' (Mandukya 2).

Shankara (8th century CE) developed Advaita Vedanta — non-duality: atman is identical to Brahman; perceived multiplicity is maya (illusion).

Ramanuja (11th-12th century) taught Vishishtadvaita — qualified non-duality: atman is a real attribute of Brahman but distinct. Madhva (13th century) taught Dvaita — full dualism: souls and God are eternally distinct.

All three schools are valid orthodox Vedantic positions.
items.why: Hindu philosophy of self is sophisticated. Treating Hinduism as 'just polytheism' misses the metaphysical core that has shaped Indian thought for over two millennia.

items.title: Muslims believe the Quran is the direct, unchanged word of God
items.claim: How do Muslims understand the origin of the Quran?

options.text: A collection of Muhammad's wise sayings, gathered over centuries
Revealed directly by God to Muhammad through the angel Jibril (Gabriel) over 23 years (610-632 CE), to be recited and transmitted unchanged in Arabic
A revised version of the Bible adapted for Arabia
A book written by Muhammad based on his teachings

items.reveal:
The word 'Quran' comes from the Arabic root q-r-' meaning 'to recite'. The first revelation (Sura 96, 'Iqra' — Recite!) at Mount Hira around 610 CE.

The Quran was compiled in written form under Caliph Uthman (around 650 CE), with non-conforming versions destroyed to ensure a single authoritative text. Muslims regard the Arabic text — not translations — as the Quran proper.

The Hadith (sayings of Muhammad) is a distinct category, recorded by his companions, with major Sunni collections by Bukhari (d. 870) and Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (d. 875).
items.why: The Quran's status differs sharply from how Christians treat the Bible (composed by human authors under divine inspiration). Islamic theology treats every Arabic word as direct divine speech — which is why translation is always a 'meaning of' the Quran.
